Add line items. One row per service or product with a clear description, quantity and unit price. The amount and totals calculate automatically.
Add your business details. Enter your name, email and address. Include your tax or VAT ID if you have one. Upload a logo once and it is remembered for future invoices.
Address it to the right person. Ask who processes payments before you start the project and put that email on the invoice.
Bill to – the parent's name and email, with the student in the notes ("Sessions for Maya, Year 10 Maths").
Cancellation or no-show fees – only if agreed in advance, and named plainly.
Change orders – anything outside the original scope, with the date the client approved it.
Check the invoice number and dates. QuickInvoice suggests the next sequential number, today's date and a due date 14 days out. Adjust the due date to match the terms you agreed on.
Commercial contracts – "Office cleaning, 3 visits/week, June" as one line, with square footage in the description.
Concepts – "Logo concepts, 3 directions" as one line.
Day rate: quantity is days; note half days as 0.5.
Deep clean, move-in/move-out – a flat fee line, plus add-ons like oven, fridge, windows or carpet on their own lines.
Deliverables – prints, albums and USB drives with quantity and unit price.
Discovery / creative brief – a flat fee or hours.
Disposal, parking, mileage – pass-through costs on their own lines.
Download the PDF. Click Download PDF, pick Save as PDF in the print dialog and send the file to your client. Click Save invoice to keep a copy in your history.
Extras – extra revision rounds, rush delivery, SEO research or image sourcing as separate lines, not buried in a higher rate.
Fill in the client. Use the exact legal name of the company or person paying you, plus the email of the person who handles payments.
Final files and brand guide – one line each; it reminds clients what they received.
Follow up on a schedule. A friendly reminder on the due date and a firmer one seven days later recovers most late invoices without damaging the relationship.
Hourly work such as editing or interviews: quantity in hours.
Hourly – quantity in hours; note the number of cleaners if you bill per person-hour.
Hourly: quantity is hours, unit price your rate. Round to the quarter hour and attach a timesheet on large engagements.
Invoice immediately. Send the invoice the day the work is delivered. Every day of delay on your side becomes a day of delay on theirs.
Keep terms short and specific. Net 14 gets paid faster than Net 30, and a due date like "15 November 2026" gets paid faster than "within 14 days".
Labor – one line per task ("Framing – 16 hrs × $65"). Hours as quantity, rate as unit price.
Labor – per task ("Replace kitchen faucet – 1.5 hrs × $75") rather than one lump of hours.
Line items by workstream: "Discovery workshop – 2 days × $1,800", "Implementation support – 34 hrs × $220".
Materials – major items with quantity and unit cost. If you add markup, bake it into the price or show a "Materials handling 10%" line; don't hide it.
Materials – workbooks or exam papers at cost.
Mention late fees politely. A line such as "1.5% monthly late fee applies after the due date" is standard and legal in most places.
Offer more than one payment method. A bank transfer is cheapest for you, but a card or PayPal option removes friction for small clients.
One line per article with the working title, e.g. "Blog: 10 Remote Onboarding Tips (1,200 words)".
One line per session – "Maths – Mon 3 Jun, 16:00" with duration as quantity (1 or 1.5) and your hourly rate as unit price, so parents can match it to their calendar.
PO number, SOW or contract reference in the notes; many companies auto-reject invoices without it.
Packages – bill a 10-session block as one line and track used sessions in the notes.

Parts and materials – each with quantity and unit price. If you mark up parts, include it in the price or show it as a line; hidden markup is what triggers disputes when the customer finds the receipt price online.
Per-word work – quantity is the word count, unit price your rate. Per-piece work uses quantity 1 and the flat fee.
Permits, dump fees, equipment rental – pass-through costs on their own lines.
Post-production – retouching and culling billed per image or per hour.
Purchase order or brief reference in the notes; invoices without it stall.
Recurring residential – one line per visit with the date ("Standard clean – Tue 4 Jun"), or quantity 4 × the visit price for a monthly invoice.
Reimbursable expenses at cost on separate lines, receipts sent alongside.
Retainer already paid – entered as a fixed discount so the balance due is obvious.
Retainer: one line, quantity 1, "Monthly advisory retainer – July 2026". If you track hours against it, mention hours used and remaining in the notes; it heads off questions about value.
Revision rounds – included rounds at zero, extra rounds at your rate, so the client sees what was free.
Service period – "Consulting services, 1–30 June 2026".
Session fee as one line, with hours as the quantity if you bill hourly.
Set tax, discount and shipping. Enter your tax rate as a percentage, and any discount as a percentage or a fixed amount.
Shoot details – date, location and type (wedding, headshots, product) in the notes.
Stock images, fonts, printing – pass-through costs at cost or your stated markup.
Supplies – only if agreed; most clients expect them included.
The client's legal name and the billing contact's email, not just your manager's.
Travel and expenses – mileage, parking, second-shooter fees.
Trip or call-out charge – one line, quantity 1. Say whether it includes the first hour.
Usage or licensing for commercial work, stating term and media (web only, print, 12 months).
Usage rights – a separate line stating scope ("Full copyright transfer on payment" or "Web and social use, 2 years").
Your legal entity name and tax ID (EIN, VAT or ABN) in the business section.
